1:
Why the chapter stands here at all is what they explain first. Clarke calls it evidently connected with the thirty-sixth, and is blunt about the arrangement — another instance of shameless transposition, since the discourse was delivered in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, years before Jerusalem fell, and being a simple appendage to that chapter should have been inserted there. Henry offers a reason for the misplacement rather than a complaint: the story should have been subjoined to the thirty-sixth, but having reference to a private person it is thrown to the end of the book, as Paul's epistle to Philemon is put after his other epistles. Calvin explains the whole book on the same principle. Prophetic books were not written in the order we now read them; when a prophet had preached and committed a summary of his doctrine to writing he fixed it to the doors of the Temple, and scribes collected the summaries, out of which the extant volumes were made — so that this book was not written by Jeremiah himself but is collected summaries afterwards formed into one volume.

Keil and Delitzsch work on the date and on a participle. The word came in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch was writing out, or had written out, the prophecies uttered up to that time; the infinitive need not mean the word came while he was still writing, since it may equally mean when he was ready with the writing, and Hitzig is wrong to reject Movers's rendering as misleading. The words Baruch was writing can only be the addresses of Jeremiah, which is why some infer that this small piece stood last in the roll originally prepared under Jehoiakim. Gill notes that Baruch was the prophet's amanuensis, and that Jeremiah spoke not of himself but in the name of the Lord; Calvin adds that Baruch was not only scribe but disciple.

What Baruch's cry meant Henry sets out with some sympathy. He was a young man setting out in the world, willing to serve God and his prophet, but when it came to suffering he was desirous to be excused; being ingenious and a scholar he stood fair for preferment, and to be driven into a corner and in danger of a prison was a great disappointment, since in reading the roll publicly he had hoped to gain reputation. Gill hears the same collapse in the words — what will become of me? I am ruined and undone — and thinks he said it in his heart if not with his lips. Wesley supplies the occasion, that on Baruch's reading the prophecies both he and Jeremiah were advised to hide themselves, which probably disturbed him and made him lament his condition; Clarke observes that Jeremiah's enemies became his too, so that he needed these promises of support, the king having commanded that both be taken.

Calvin is the least indulgent of them. The prophet accosts Baruch to fill his mind with holy fear, and so correct the sinful fear that impeded him in strenuously serving God — for Baruch no doubt wished to withdraw from his office, as men do who, finding themselves unequal to a task that presses them, seek hiding-places and become runagates. It was highly honourable to be scribe to a prophet, the same thing as receiving words from the mouth of an angel; and it was unworthy and disgraceful for a holy servant of God to complain of his own misery when the office itself was evidence of singular favour. What is condemned here, Calvin says, is ingratitude: Baruch exclaimed that he was miserable when he ought to have counted it a singular happiness that God had called him to that work.
4:
The answer begins by putting Baruch's trouble beside a larger one. Gill notes the words are spoken to Jeremiah, an order as to what he should say to Baruch in the Lord's name; Clarke reduces the message to its certainty, that God will fulfil all the threatenings contained in the very roll Baruch had written, and destroy the whole land. Calvin makes the comparison the whole point of the reproof. The prophet shows he was not roused against Baruch by private displeasure but had only carried God's message; the cause of the reproof was that Baruch loved himself too much and wished to evade danger when God had ordered him into the conflict. God mentions the whole people deliberately, as though he had said: dost thou wish to be deemed of more importance than the whole people, and is thy life of more value than the wellbeing of the whole community? It was a disgrace, Calvin says, to prefer himself to the people, and even to the Temple and the worship of God; and when God's severity was ready to fall on all of them, Baruch ought not to have made so much account of his own life.

On the great things sought, Calvin presses the same balance harder. The words for thyself are put emphatically, God setting Baruch in one scale and in the other the whole people with the temple and divine worship: shall thy state be eminent while the temple is burnt with fire, the land laid waste, most men perish and the remnant are driven into exile? Art thou alone to be deemed sacred, alone exempt from loss and trouble? God's purpose was to shame him for preferring a frail life to so many glorious things; and having made Baruch his own judge he immediately restrains him, since we know how men from self-love seek their own indulgence.

What the great things were the others try to name. Gill lists riches and wealth, honour and esteem, peace and prosperity — none of them to be sought when the whole nation was to be involved in a general calamity; and he guesses that Baruch had expected his reading of the roll before the princes to prefer him at court, advancing him to some post in which he might acquire wealth and live in plenty all his days, though the very roll he read foretold the nation's ruin. He adds that the Jews restrain the phrase to the gift of prophecy, which they suppose Baruch sought and which was not to be enjoyed outside the land of Canaan. Clarke divides the refusal in two: nothing better can be expected of this people, so Baruch's hopes of them are vain and no national amendment should be looked for till national judgments have come; and as for benefit to himself, let it be enough that God has determined to preserve his life. Wesley puts the rebuke as a question — dost thou expect what none who fears God is like to meet with? — and takes the calamity to fall on the whole nation.

The promise that closes the chapter Clarke reads as a proverb with a sting of comfort in it. To have one's life given for a prey is to have it as a spoil is had, gained from a vanquished enemy and kept with pleasure as the proof and reward of a man's own valour; so Baruch's life should be doubly precious to him, not only for the dangers through which God had brought him safely but for the services he had rendered, the consolations he had received, and God's continual interposition on his behalf — all dearer to him than the spoils of a beaten foe to the hero who had overcome in battle. Spoil, he adds, may signify unlooked-for gain.
